implementation_notes: As in JavaScript, the platform has no heap; TypeScript adds typing over a library or a hand-rolled heap. The typing helps: a PriorityQueue<T> interface with enqueue(item, priority), dequeue(), peek() gives a scheduler a total, mockable contract, and a sorted-array implementation satisfies it just as well as a binary heap for small N - which is the right choice below a few thousand entries given V8's array performance. For large N or frequent priority changes, use a heap with an index map so decrease-key is O(log n) rather than O(n). In Node.js, wrap the queue in a mutex: the event loop gives no protection across await points, so a dequeue and an enqueue can interleave and lose an item.
idiom_name: PriorityQueue<T> interface over a sorted array (small N) or an indexed binary heap (large N, decrease-key)
pitfalls: Array.prototype.sort on every push, or a linear scan for the minimum, gives O(n^2) over a run - the most common wrong implementation.
No decrease-key in a naive implementation: a Dijkstra frontier needs an index map, or lazy deletion with a stale check on dequeue.
Ties on priority need the monotonic seq field, or the comparison falls through and the order becomes arbitrary.
The event loop gives no atomicity across await points - a dequeue and an enqueue can interleave in Node.js and lose an item unless guarded by a mutex.
